items.title: Metal band Genitorturers claims a Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines remake is coming, getting a dozen crusty nerds way too worked up
items.author: ted.litchfield@futurenet.com (Ted Litchfield)
items.summary: Original Story: This one is thin, man, but it has to do with one of my favorite games of all time, while the circumstances of the rumor are just kind of neat
items.text:
Original Story: This one is thin, man, but it has to do with one of my favorite games of all time, while the circumstances of the rumor are just kind of neat and weird, even if it turns out to be nothing. User Few_Interview8222 on the Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines subreddit reported back from a Genitorturers show in Brooklyn, New York. Partway through the set, the band supposedly told the crowd that a VtMB remake is happening.

Genitorturers played at Brooklyn's The Meadows as part of their "Live + Lewd Tour" on October 15. We've reached out to both rights-holder Activision (one of several, it's complicated) and Genitorturers' representation, and will update this story if we hear back.

Why would an industrial metal band started in Orlando in 1986 have this information?

In addition to a killer score by Rik Schaffer, Bloodlines featured wonderfully era-appropriate licensed tracks from metal bands⁠—they were mostly used as diegetic music in the nightclubs and bars of Los Angeles. The Genitorturers track Lecher Bitch was the pitch-perfect theme of The Last Round, a downtown LA dive bar frequented by the Anarch faction of vampires.

What if they're wrong?

Multiple commenters on the Reddit thread point out that this could have been a confused, untimely, misinterpreted, or all of the above reference to last year's Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2. It's the sort of almost-but-not-quite thing you might expect from an artist with tangential awareness of a secondary fanbase they picked up over the years.

A VtMB remake is also the sort of project you could see getting pingponged around between various actors and stakeholders: started, stopped, shopped around, etc. It'd be a situation ripe for collaborators on the periphery acting on outdated information.

What if they're right?

Rad! I think? It'd depend on who's doing it. More and more, I'm beginning to distrust anyone not named "Nightdive" when it comes to commercial remasters. See also: The recent Shogun 2 debacle and the fate of Deus Ex Remastered.

Bloodlines is such a wild, janky, PC gaming package that Nightdive is the only studio I'd trust to not only do a remaster right, but also to bring on legendary modder Werner "Wesp5" Spahl, the man who's been keeping Bloodlines alive with one of the most impactful unofficial patch projects in gaming. A more ground-up remake would offer equally daunting challenges, like matching the one-of-a-kind mood and look Troika managed to evoke.

Why should you care?

Bloodlines is one of my very favorite games and an incredible RPG that's well worth your time. To the uninitiated, I like to pitch it as an evolutionary missing link between 2D Fallout and New Vegas. Bloodlines boasts the open-ended design and reactivity of Fallout in 3D for the very first time (Bloodlines leads Leonard Boyarsky and Jason Anderson were senior talent on Fallout 1).

Unlike New Vegas' wide open world, however, Bloodlines had a more linear, but still loose sequence of zones on a world map to explore. Bloodlines' Y2K, gothic, noir interpretation of Los Angeles is one of the coolest worlds ever presented in an RPG.

A Nightdive treatment would be my preferred outcome: build on Wesp5's work and compensate him accordingly, then make it more accessible on more platforms at a modest markup over the original game. Bloodlines 1 can be had for $20 on Steam and GOG, but it's practically always on sale.

Even if it turns out to be nothing, this is still just a neat, newsworthy little incident to behold—Genitorturers shouting out an obscure, beloved RPG like this 22 years later, and maybe getting a couple genre nerds like me a little too excited on the way.

items.text:
Updated
Oct 19, 2026, 5:11 AM EDT

Diego Pineda has been a devout storyteller his whole life. He has self-published a fantasy novel and a book of short stories, and is actively working on publishing his second novel.
A lifelong fan of watching movies and talking about them endlessly, he writes reviews and analyses on his Instagram page dedicated to cinema, and occasionally on his blog. His favorite filmmakers are Andrei Tarkovsky and Charlie Chaplin. He loves modern Mexican cinema and thinks it's tragically underappreciated.
Other interests of Diego's include reading, gaming, roller coasters, writing reviews on his Letterboxd account (username: DPP_reviews), and going down rabbit holes of whatever topic he's interested in at any given point.

Animation is one of the most powerful kinds of media that movies and television have to offer. As a storytelling device that's pretty much visually limitless, it has allowed artists throughout the years to craft some of the most imaginative and expansive TV shows ever made. Likewise, its unique visual capabilities allow animation to deliver some of the most emotionally hard-hitting narratives that the small screen is able to contain.

From kid-friendly fare like Steven Universe to animation aimed directly at grown-ups like Primal, a surprising number of the most heartbreaking TV shows in history are animated. Some of them have tearjerkers interspersed between mostly joyful scenes, while others are straight-up depressing throughout. If anything, these series prove that animation can be as emotionally complex and moving as live-action.

15
'Monkey Dust' (2003–2005)

Image via BBC

Sketch comedy has delivered several of the greatest adult animated shows in history, and the BBC's Monkey Dust is undoubtedly one of the most underrated. This pitch-black comedy satirizes and pokes fun at British society and tabloid culture, but what makes it one of the best animated shows you've never heard of is just how universally hilarious it can be.

But as often as its unashamed handling of taboo topics can result in absolute hilarity for people who enjoy dark humor, it can also be a surprisingly poignant and emotionally affecting series. Its scathing satire can at times be so cynical and pessimistic that one can't help but be saddened by its reflection of the horrors of contemporary society.

14
'Fired on Mars' (2023)

Image via Max

HBO Max technically never officially announced Fired on Mars' cancellation, though fans have grown convinced that after three years of no news on its future, it has likely been quietly shelved. Regardless, one thing is certain: This sci-fi comedy about a graphic designer who travels to the Red Planet to work for a tech startup, based on creators Nate Sherman and Nick Vokey's 2016 short film, is one of the best adult animated shows of the 2020s so far.

In its depiction of a painfully relatable satirization of corporate culture and a sci-fi story imbued with existential dread, Fired on Mars created a tale that can often be unexpectedly sad and anxiety-inducing. The show overall is an awful lot of fun, but when it specifically sets out to convey the desperately depressing situation its protagonist finds himself in, it definitely works.

13
'Carol & the End of the World' (2023)

Image via Netflix

Netflix has made many great miniseries over the years, but few of them are as unique as the adult animated dramedy Carol & the End of the World, arguably one of the best animated miniseries of all time. The series still holds an admirable 100% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and it's entirely well-deserved, because this story, about a middle-aged woman finding comfort in mundane routine as Earth heads toward an impending planetary apocalypse, is nothing short of delightful.

Needless to say, though, Carol & the End of the World is fully aware of the inherently melancholic nature of its premise and constantly takes full advantage of it. Its comedic elements work brilliantly, but they're carefully balanced out with the feelings of isolation, numbness, and grief that naturally come with any story about the world preparing for extinction.

12
'Undone' (2019–2022)

Image via Prime Video

One of Raphael Bob-Waksberg's next ventures after the end of BoJack Horseman was co-creating Undone with Kate Purdy. This science fantasy dramedy, Amazon's first use of rotoscoping animation for a TV show, is one of the best overlooked animated shows that deserve more attention. In it, a young woman develops the ability to manipulate time after surviving a near-fatal car crash.

Like pretty much all of Bob-Waksberg's work, Undone is concerned with analyzing themes of mental illness, generational trauma, and complex family dynamics. And like pretty much all of Bob-Waksberg's work, Undone is also profoundly poignant and emotionally layered. It's an intensely surreal and emotionally heavy show, though its more hopeful and amusing elements are a refreshing way to balance out the bleakness.

11
'Bluey' (2018–Present)

Image via ABC Kids

Bluey is truly a special kind of show, the type that comes along only once in a generation. While it's the perfect series for its target audience — children — it often feels that it's aimed at the little ones' parents just as much, which is what's gotten it to IMDb's Top 10 of the highest-rated shows on the site. It follows the slice-of-life adventures of an Australian blue heeler cattle dog puppy as she has fun and learns valuable lessons with her family and friends.

Colorful, vibrant, with great role models, and with a delightful sense of humor, Bluey is many children's favorite show for a very good reason. However, adults paying close enough attention will often be treated to subtle yet powerful depictions of topics as deep as miscarriages, mental health, and grief. This results in some of the most potent bittersweet moments that anyone will ever be able to find in kids' media.

10
'Futurama' (1999–Present)

Image via FOX

Sci-fi sitcoms aren't all that common, but among the few that do exist, there are some that are beyond iconic. Futurama is one such series. In it, pizza delivery boy Philip J. Fry is accidentally frozen in 1999 and thawed out on New Year's Eve of 2999. With a team of friends, he travels on countless intergalactic adventures where the gang gets into shenanigans with potentially terrible consequences.

Futurama is one of the funniest sci-fi comedies that the small screen has ever been graced with. It has some of the genre's most entertaining characters, most fun storylines, and most intellectual humor (the writers created a literal language for the show). However, it also has some of the saddest moments of any animated comedy, including what might just be the saddest sitcom episode ever in Season 5's "Jurassic Bark." It's a delightful show overall, but it's also not afraid to hit its audience right in the feels.

9
'Steven Universe' (2013–2019)

Image via Cartoon Network

One of the most beloved shows Cartoon Network has ever put out, Steven Universe is about a team of intergalactic warriors fighting to protect the Earth. However, the combination of three highly trained beings and one quirky young boy leaves the team struggling to overcome the dangerous scenarios they're faced with. With phenomenal music, beautiful animation, and unprecedented representation, it's no wonder why Steven Universe is so well-liked.

Sure, the show's colorful aesthetic and playful tone make it a blast of fun from start to finish, but there are also surprising amounts of thematic complexity and nuance here, considering that it's a series mainly aimed at tweens and young teens. With its highly likable characters being put through some of the most emotional episodes that have ever aired on Cartoon Network, Steven Universe gets tears out of its viewers as often as it does laughs.

Animation is one of the most powerful kinds of media that movies and television have to offer. As a storytelling device that's pretty much visually limitless, it has allowed artists throughout the years to craft some of the most imaginative and expansive TV shows ever made. Likewise, its unique visual capabilities allow animation to deliver some of the most emotionally hard-hitting narratives that the small screen is able to contain.

From kid-friendly fare like Steven Universe to animation aimed directly at grown-ups like Primal, a surprising number of the most heartbreaking TV shows in history are animated. Some of them have tearjerkers interspersed between mostly joyful scenes, while others are straight-up depressing throughout. If anything, these series prove that animation can be as emotionally complex and moving as live-action.

The Legend Of Zelda: A Link To The Past Is Officially Returning In New Collection

Published Oct 19, 2026, 2:00 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

The Legend of Zelda really is a series like no other, with an unprecedented period of longevity and relevance at the very top of the industry. For 40 years now, Nintendo has been bringing us memorable experiences and some of the most enjoyable games to play that you'll find anywhere, and that's why so much is being celebrated around the 40th anniversary this year.

A big part of those celebrations has been taking a moment to remember the games that started it all, and there are plenty of excellent options to choose from. Arguably the best of the bunch is A Link to the Past, the third game in the series and still one of the most beloved to date. Now, a new set of releases is on the way that includes that game as part of its wider offering attached to the franchise, and you can pick it up for quite cheap if you're in the right place at the right time.

In case you missed it, Japanese toy manufacturer Takara Tomy confirmed the upcoming release of The Legend of Zelda: Historical Charms collection. These essentially function as keyrings or small collectibles, and they can be claimed via gachapon machines in Japan. This obviously adds an element of gambling to proceedings, but given that you're going to be paying around $2 per go, you shouldn't need to spend too much money to pick up the one you want or, indeed, the entire collection.

There are 12 charms to collect in total, with each one shaped like the iconic Triforce from the series, as well as featuring a design from an individual game. The list of games memorialized in the new release is as follows:

The Legend of Zelda

Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link

A Link to the Past

Ocarina of Time

Majora's Mask

The Wind Waker

Twilight Princess

Skyward Sword

Link's Awakening

Breath of the Wild

Tears of the Kingdom

Echoes of Wisdom

They are set to launch this month, though obviously you will need to be in Japan to take advantage of them. That said, if you do happen to be over there any time soon, they should be pretty widely available and easy to find. There's no news yet on whether they are planning for a release anywhere else, but it's unlikely given the price. A Link to the Past is, of course, the game that truly defined the classic Zelda formula as we know it today, and is easily one of the greatest SNES games of all time.

Elsewhere, fans of The Legend of Zelda have so much to look forward to. The first big release that everyone will likely be playing is the Ocarina of Time Remake, which drops next month, just a couple of weeks before GTA VI. That leads into the arrival of the big budget feature film adaptation, which is set to show us the series in a whole new medium for the first time.

items.title: “Tulsa King,” and Stallone, Start to Show Their Age in Season 4
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting
items.text:
Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting somewhere between “Yellowstone” and “Get Shorty” in its tale of a New York goombah (Sylvester Stallone) starting his criminal enterprise all over again in Oklahoma, the show has spent three seasons simply letting its bulging cast of characters engage in soap-opera theatrics, squaring off against rival gang members and, in this last set of episodes, a vindictive bourbon distiller played by Robert Patrick. (Spoiler alert: Sly burns him at the stake in the season finale. I guess it’s the only way to be sure with the T-1000.) But in season four, “Tulsa King” finally feels like it’s getting lost in the literal and metaphorical sauce.

After taking over Patrick’s distillery, Dwight “The General” Manfredi (Stallone) is finally ready to legitimize his enterprises (well, some of them) and settle down with his girlfriend of three seasons, Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany). Unfortunately, mysterious circumstances arise at the end of the season premiere that leave Dwight in deep mourning and unsure where his businesses stand with the government. That latter concern is compounded by the elevation of lieutenant governor Amanda Clark (Gretchen Mol), a by-the-books do-gooder who knows Dwight’s game and wants to shut him down permanently, to the top office.

That’s not Dwight’s only concern, of course; his old mafia family in New York City keeps gunning for the profits he’s been building in the Southwest, especially now that his old nemesis, Quiet Ray (James Russo), is fully in charge. What’s more, a greedy German AI tech bro (Flula Borg) is threatening to take Margaret’s horse ranch by eminent domain to turn the land into a data center.

(L-R): Scarlet Stallone as Spencer, Martin Starr as Bodhi, and Jay Will as Tyson in Tulsa King, episode 1, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

All these conflicts and more stud “Tulsa King”‘s new season, and that’s not even getting into Bodhi’s (Martin Starr) flirtation with wine forgery, or Tyson’s (Jay Will) burgeoning rap career. And let’s not forget Dwight’s unsteady alliance with government spook Musso (Kevin Pollak) from last season and how that dovetails with Dwight’s existing animus with fellow capo Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo). Hey, there are a lot of aging character actors to pay; we gotta give them something to do, right? We should be thankful Samuel L. Jackson isn’t here to soak up more screen time, as he’s supposedly off building his own spinoff down in New Orleans.

“Tulsa King,” at this point, is more overstuffed than a turducken, with a cast so bloated that the gang is juggling at least three or four different schemes at once. Even Sly is getting a little tired; sure, some of that is Dwight’s puffed-up grief, but some of it is the older actor slowing down. (The show even writes a cane into Dwight’s ensemble; it’s passed off as an occasional knee injury that flares up from time to time, but I get the feeling that cane’s here to stay.) Even Sly coasting is compelling enough to watch, but you can tell the rest of the cast has to shore up their game to help carry this thing. This is especially true of Annabella Sciorra’s Joanne, Dwight’s enterprising sister and partner in crime, who slowly becomes the show’s heart and soul.

Gretchen Mol as Amanda Clark in Tulsa King, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

In fact, you get the most enjoyment from showrunner Dave Erickson and his writing team’s occasional lapses into the ridiculous. Italian enforcer pals Goodie (Chris Caldovino) and Vince (Vincent Piazza) shoot their way out of a white supremacist meeting at a restaurant they happen to be eating at; “You just got robbed by two swarthy Mediterraneans!” they shout as they leave. Dwight mournfully asks an AI chatbot whether God exists, and the scene is treated as if it’s dispensing therapeutic wisdom from on high. Someone gets their head crushed in the jaws of a fossilized dinosaur skull. In these scenes, “Tulsa King” ekes out a kind of campy enjoyment. It’s just a shame you have to sift through so many diluted storylines to get there. (The less said about the budding romance between Garrett Hedlund’s Mitch and Scarlet Stallone’s Spencer, the better.)

It’d be dishonest to claim “Tulsa King” doesn’t offer consistent diversion, even amid the myriad components of Dwight’s business empire and all the spinning plates therein. But this season’s villains don’t compel (including everyone’s favorite “My Son Hunter” director Robert Davi as a creaky enforcer who looks like he can barely stand, let alone take out fools), and so many of the plot threads feel like filler to give Dwight’s bloated entourage things to do. The bulk of the show’s charm falls squarely on Stallone’s broad shoulders, and even he’s starting to lose a step. Here’s hoping the show can get its affairs in order in an already-announced season five, or this vital leg of the Taylor Sheridan universe will go, well, the way of the dinosaur.

Full season screened for review. Premieres October 16th on Paramount+.

items.title: PlayStation 6 Price Update Is Bad News For The Next Generation
items.author: Tom Wilson
items.summary:
PlayStation 6 Price Update Is Bad News For The Next Generation

Published Oct 19, 2026, 6:08 AM EDT

Tom Wilson is a Gaming Features Writer at Screen Rant.
items.text:
PlayStation 6 Price Update Is Bad News For The Next Generation

Published Oct 19, 2026, 6:08 AM EDT

Tom Wilson is a Gaming Features Writer at Screen Rant. Over the past five years, Tom has worked as the Editor-in-Chief at The Game Crater, as a Staff Writer for GamingIntel, a List Writer at TheGamer, and, of course, as a Senior Writer at ScreenRant. Tom has experience writing reviews, guides, news, and features, and has been responsible for teams of writers, training them and editing their work.
Tom graduated with a Masters in Multimedia Journalism, and has since gone on to build up his portfolio of games journalism work.

There have always been concerns about the next generation of consoles, specifically the PlayStation 6. There is the incremental improvement of video game graphics rendering a new generation largely redundant, the slow pace of game development resulting in fewer exclusives and thus fewer reasons to invest in a new console, and the high price enforced by ongoing real-world complications prohibiting the vast majority of consumers from purchasing it. However, it is perhaps this latter point that proves to be the most damning, the very thing that will truly determine the fate of Sony's new console.

Even if it produces a vastly superior image and is packed with new exclusives, the PlayStation 6 will simply collect dust in warehouses should its price point not meet the realistic expectations of consumers suffering from a seemingly endless cost-of-living crisis. Unfortunately, the PlayStation 6's controversial price just got another update, and it is looking as dour as it always has, a stark realization that feels as if it foretells the end of casual gaming as we know it.

The PlayStation 6's potential price point has been fluctuating for quite some time, with analysts, leakers, and the like all throwing their hat into the proverbial ring with figures based on estimates or hearsay. However, by collating all of this information and various reliable reports, we can likely accurately gauge just how much the PS6 will cost. Unfortunately, it would appear that previous estimates, made prior to the boom in AI and the sudden price hike in assorted hardware, are wrong, with new figures pointing to the PlayStation 6 costing $1,000 or more.

This is based on a new leak from renowned hardware leaker KeplerL2. This leaker has been revealing information regarding the PS6 and its purported costs for quite some time, initially claiming it would cost the consumer around $699.99, a subsidized cost based on now-antiquated production costs of $760. KeplerL2 later revealed that the cost to make a PS6 had risen dramatically to $960 as a consequence of AI companies' stranglehold on the necessary parts. Now, in a recent NeoGAF forum, KeplerL2 said that the cost of "RAM + NAND alone is over $680."

This, coupled with the fact that Sony previously stated (as reported by VGC) that it doesn't plan on "selling hardware at significant losses" and that customers should "fully understand the value we provide in relation to pricing," likely means that we're looking at a $1,000 next-gen console, at the very least. RAM and NAND only cover the console's memory, which, while a significant part of the material costs, doesn't include other requisite components such as the GPU and CPU.

Even if Sony were to subsidize the cost, it would still cost the consumer nearly double what the PS5 did back in 2020. With analysts seemingly unanimous in agreeing that the cost of the PS6 could exceed $1,000, the future of next-gen gaming is looking bleak. Of course, Sony could push back the PS6's tentative release date of 2027, but that could end up costing it a fortune, something it may likely look to offset by simply shipping the console at a prohibitively high price.

It remains to be seen what Sony's next steps will be, although one can only imagine it is desperate to recoup a little goodwill after burning it all with its physical media debacle. Perhaps the PlayStation 6 will be impressive enough to warrant the price tag, but for $1,000, simply offering a console that produces better visuals and faster load times won't be enough, as the PS5 and its Pro model have more or less been doing that for over half a decade.

items.text:
Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Reviews Reach High Not Seen Since 2010's Black Ops

Published Oct 19, 2026, 5:50 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

We are just a few days away from the launch of Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and as the 23rd installment in the Call of Duty franchise, it is going to have to do a lot to stand out amongst the rest, especially with more recent entries being criticized for their lack of ambition.

However, it seems as though Infinity Ward and Activision have nothing to worry about, as critic reviews see the brand-new Call of Duty installment hit highs not seen since the launch of 2010's Call of Duty: Black Ops.

Set to launch on 23 October for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S, Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is the fourth and final entry in the rebooted Modern Warfare sub-series. With its last entry, 2023's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III, being met with mixed reviews due to its poor campaign, it seems as though Infinity Ward went back to the drawing table, and has managed to finish off the spin-off series with a bang.

As such, our very own Rob Keyes was lucky enough to visit Infinity Ward back in May, and it is here that his hands-on preview revealed that Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was a major reset for the franchise. He wrote:

Infinity Ward is also introducing new systems like Apex Attachments, gameplay-altering endgame weapon upgrades, and Gunny, a smart Gunsmith assistant that automatically generates weapon builds around specific playstyles from your available attachments. I have much more to share on Modern Warfare 4’s multiplayer, including its new movement systems, the complete list of weapons available at launch, franchise-first tech, and what I played during my visit to Infinity Ward, in this separate deep dive. I promise, it's awesome.

Now, a few months on, and we are days away from the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and according to a recent Twitter/X post by CharlieIntel, an account dedicated to all things Call of Duty, this brand-new entry "is currently the best-rated Call of Duty title on Steam since 2010's Call of Duty: Black Ops."

You may be wondering how this could be the case if the game does not release until 23 October. Well, back on 16 October, purchasing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 early would unlock access to the campaign, allowing players to dive into the action ahead of the game's full launch.

So, if you think about it, these rave reviews correspond to the upcoming campaign, more so than the all-important multiplayer mode, which is set to unlock later this week. As such, those reviews could definitely change depending on how well this mode is received, but, for now, it seems as though Infinity Ward has taken on the feedback from previous installments and worked on the campaign.

Back on Twitter/X, fans shared their thoughts on CharlieIntel's post, with one writing, "The power of a great campaign", whilst another said, "Let's wait until multiplayer releases. Those reviews will plummit."

It remains to be seen what the reviews for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 will look like in a month from now. In the meantime, it seems as though the future is looking bright for the final installment in the Modern Warfare sub-series.

We are just a few days away from the launch of Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and as the 23rd installment in the Call of Duty franchise, it is going to have to do a lot to stand out amongst the rest, especially with more recent entries being criticized for their lack of ambition.

However, it seems as though Infinity Ward and Activision have nothing to worry about, as critic reviews see the brand-new Call of Duty installment hit highs not seen since the launch of 2010's Call of Duty: Black Ops.

Set to launch on 23 October for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S, Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is the fourth and final entry in the rebooted Modern Warfare sub-series. With its last entry, 2023's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III, being met with mixed reviews due to its poor campaign, it seems as though Infinity Ward went back to the drawing table, and has managed to finish off the spin-off series with a bang.

As such, our very own Rob Keyes was lucky enough to visit Infinity Ward back in May, and it is here that his hands-on preview revealed that Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was a major reset for the franchise. He wrote:

Infinity Ward is also introducing new systems like Apex Attachments, gameplay-altering endgame weapon upgrades, and Gunny, a smart Gunsmith assistant that automatically generates weapon builds around specific playstyles from your available attachments. I have much more to share on Modern Warfare 4’s multiplayer, including its new movement systems, the complete list of weapons available at launch, franchise-first tech, and what I played during my visit to Infinity Ward, in this separate deep dive. I promise, it's awesome.

Now, a few months on, and we are days away from the launch of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and according to a recent Twitter/X post by CharlieIntel, an account dedicated to all things Call of Duty, this brand-new entry "is currently the best-rated Call of Duty title on Steam since 2010's Call of Duty: Black Ops."

You may be wondering how this could be the case if the game does not release until 23 October. Well, back on 16 October, purchasing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 early would unlock access to the campaign, allowing players to dive into the action ahead of the game's full launch.

Consider this your permission slip to think a little weird. The Aquarius Moon favors oddball ideas, so the plan that sounds ridiculous at first might be the smartest one you’ve had in months. Let the skeptics catch up later. Love and money get a reality check as Pluto squares Venus, stargazer, and anyone coasting on your goodwill could get found out. If a deal or a date feels off, believe yourself. Mercury goes retrograde Saturday, so lock in plans and double-check the details. Tempers could fray late tonight while the Moon opposes Mars, especially among the overtired. Skip the petty arguments with loved ones and save your fire for what actually counts tomorrow.

Read your horoscope for the week, and see what the stars have in store for your sign today.

Aries: March 21 – April 19

Expect at least one person to test your patience before bed. The Aquarius Moon opposes Mars tonight, so a stray hot take could get under your skin, Aries. Saturn’s trine to Mars is past its peak but still backing your self-control. Let them write their paragraph-long reply. Leave them on read and go to sleep. Wake up the undefeated champ of keeping your cool.

Aries monthly horoscope

Taurus: April 20 – May 20

Somebody has a very persuasive pitch ready for you, and your stomach already knows the answer. Pluto’s square to Venus peaks tomorrow, so pressure around money or love is cranked up, Taurus. Luckily, Venus is conjunct Haumea, tuning up your instincts. With Venus retrograde, take your time. That famous stubborn streak is a superpower today. Smile politely and say you’ll think about it.

Taurus monthly horoscope

Gemini: May 21 – June 20

Those half-typed texts sitting in your drafts won’t send themselves. Mercury is slowing down ahead of Saturday’s retrograde, Gemini, so wrap up loose conversations while signals are still crisp. Jupiter’s square to Mercury tempts you to start five new threads instead. Resist. The Aquarius Moon trines your sign, giving you the charm to close each one gracefully. Hit send, then enjoy the empty inbox.

Gemini monthly horoscope

Cancer: June 21 – July 22

Weirdly, other people’s drama might bounce right off you today. The Moon moves through cool, detached Aquarius and trines Uranus, giving you a break from feeling everything for everyone, Cancer. Enjoy the vacation. An evening sextile to Saturn helps you finish chores without guilt. Late tonight, the Moon opposes Mars, so save heavy talks for another day. Tomorrow your big heart reopens for business.

Cancer monthly horoscope

Leo: July 23 – August 22

One unimpressed coworker can rattle even the proudest lion. Pluto starts squaring the Sun today, Leo, so someone might push back on your ideas or poke at your ego. Venus is also moving toward the Sun, though, giving you extra charm to work with. Skip the power struggle. Win them over with warmth instead. A little curiosity about their side goes a long way.

Leo monthly horoscope

Virgo: August 23 – September 22

Today’s least glamorous act of self-care is a full backup of your phone and laptop. Mercury is tapping the brakes before this weekend’s retrograde, Virgo, and tech hiccups love a distracted user. Jupiter’s square to Mercury makes everything feel bigger than it is, including small glitches. Pick the boring safeguards first. Future you, staring at a frozen screen next week, will feel incredibly smug.

Virgo monthly horoscope

Libra: September 23 – October 22

Quick tally of the last five plans: you made every single one. If that sounds familiar, Libra, Pluto’s square to Venus is bringing that imbalance to the surface right before tomorrow’s peak. Venus also teams up with Haumea, so trust the gut feeling you keep politely ignoring. Ask for more effort, kindly and clearly. The ones who value you will gladly match your energy.

Libra monthly horoscope

Scorpio: October 23 – November 21

No judgment if you wake up in the middle of the night and look up an old flame. The Moon joins Pluto early, pulling buried feelings up, Scorpio, and Pluto’s square to Venus amps up the urge to know everything. Curiosity is natural. Obsession is optional. Close the tab and put the phone face down. Your peace is hotter than any answer.

Scorpio monthly horoscope

Sagittarius: November 22 – December 21

A friend’s bold new life choice is about to test your poker face. Jupiter’s square to Mercury makes your honest opinions come out bigger and blunter than intended, Sagittarius. Jupiter’s sextile to the Sun is fading but leaves enough warmth to soften the delivery. Lead with a question before offering a verdict. Your truth is most welcome when someone asks for it.

Sagittarius monthly horoscope

Capricorn: December 22 – January 19

Credit where it’s due includes you, too. Saturn opposes Makemake, so you might find yourself championing everyone else’s wins while downplaying your own, Capricorn. Saturn’s trine to Mars is easing but still fuels your drive, and an evening Moon-Saturn sextile makes it easy to state your case calmly. Mention your contribution at the next meeting. Your hard work earned a byline.

Capricorn monthly horoscope

Aquarius: January 20 – February 18

An actual emotion may sneak past your big-brain defenses today. The Moon sits in your sign and trines Uranus, so feelings arrive as flashes of insight, Aquarius, which is the only way you trust them anyway. Uranus is retrograde, asking you to rebel against your own aloofness. Tell one person you missed them. Weird and warm is your best combo.

Aquarius monthly horoscope

Pisces: February 19 – March 20

Before agreeing to one more favor, check who keeps doing all the asking. Neptune is retrograde in bold Aries, peeling back illusions about who’s truly in your corner, Pisces. A soft overnight sextile from the Moon leaves you dreamy but intuitive, so your first impressions are spot-on. Save your generosity for people who return it. You’re allowed to say “not this time.”

Pisces monthly horoscope

This is gonna get confusing real fast, so I need everyone to lock in for the sentence you’re about to read: the devs behind Needle In A Haystack, which is a clone of the original viral haystack game, Needle In A Haystack Simulator, have accused the developers of another clone of the original haystack game, titled A Game About Needle In A Haystack, of copying their code, as the copy of the copy contains exactly the same error messages as their game “word for word.”

Even just typing that gave me a headache, so let’s rewind a bit. This isn’t the first time we’ve covered copies of Studio Bitdot’s viral haystack game, Needle In A Haystack Simulator. After several clips of Studio Bitdot’s incremental sorting sim went viral across social media in August, Steam users noticed that several similarly titled games, with inventive titles such as A Needle In a Haystack and Story of The Needle In a Haystack, had suddenly appeared on the platform overnight.

As of writing, I count at least fourteen clones of Studio Bitdot’s original game on Steam. One such game is studio NoGlyph’s Needle In A Haystack, which was released on Steam on September 29. To be clear, NoGlyph’s game doesn’t appear to be in any way vibe-coded, and, for what it’s worth, also doesn’t feature any AI disclaimers on its Steam store page.

Yesterday, on October 17, NoGlyph accused another Needle In A Haystack Simulator clone on Steam of ripping off their code: Little Field Studios’ A Game About Needle In A Haystack, which was released on October 16.

“When we looked through [A Game About Needle In A Haystack’s] files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names,” reads NoGlyph’s post on Steam. “More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn’t exist in their game.”

While NoGlyph’s post on Steam doesn’t outright accuse Little Field Studios’ clone of being vibe-coded slop, a comment from the team’s lead dev, Jahvin, on NoGlyph’s Discord confirms exactly how many pieces of its code were copied. Jahvin states that Little Field Studios’ game contains 39 “same-named methods” that are “byte-for-byte identical.”

What Jahvin describes is a classic telltale sign of Claude-assisted decompilation: taking a closed-source game and using AI to make its source code readable, then copy-pasting that code into your own game (or, more likely, asking Claude to do it for you).

While Steam users seem unsympathetic, with some referring to it as “karma” for NoGlyph’s attempt at riding off the coattails of Studio Bitdot’s original Needle In A Haystack Simulator game, the potential vibe-coding element to the story does speak to a larger issue in the indie game scene.

As GameSpark covered in a recent article, a Roblox creator cloned the upcoming indie game Escape the Walls within 24 hours of its dev showing it off to the public. The Roblox creator in question achieved this by simply using a single video of Escape the Walls on X, and then, according to GameSpark, quite brazenly bragged about how said feat was achieved: “Claude did everything for me; I just sat in my chair and watched.”

Likewise, the devs behind Drunken Goddess Reflux, Alliance Arts, announced that they had cancelled plans to release its upcoming demo on Steam. Why? Because Alliance Arts were concerned that “works imitating or replicating this game’s presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI” if Drunken Goddess Reflux’s demo was released ahead of the full game.

Sadly, it seems like this is the new normal for indie games. Unlike big AAA publishers, indie devs do not have the funding required to legally challenge every single vibe-coded ripoff of their game that appears online, so expect to see fewer demos, fewer early access titles, and, if Escape the Walls’ example is anything to go by, fewer trailers for indie games in the immediate future.

items.text:
Disk Cleanup

(Image credit: Future)Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Joe Ziegler might be best known for his role guiding the design of big competitive shooters, but his formative gaming experiences were with point-and-click adventures like King's Quest. "There was something so clever about trying to use all this knowledge about random things like fairy tales to try to solve puzzles inside of the game," he says. "It was just that 'A-ha!' moment where videogames could be these really engaging ways for you to be clever and creative."

Ziegler started out at Pandemic Studios, where he worked as a mission designer on 2009's The Saboteur. But he is best known as game director on Riot's hugely popular arena shooter Valorant, and his more recent oversight of Bungie's extraction-shooter revival of Marathon, which he assumed leadership of in March 2024 following the dismissal of former director Christopher Barret.

Following Marathon's launch, Ziegler left Bungie and is currently working on a new, unrevealed project: "My goal ultimately when I'm thinking about 'What do I direct and what do I make?' is 'Where can I make the coolest thing with the coolest people?'" he explains. "That's part of the reason I went to Bungie in the first place. And now, as I'm looking at this next thing, I'm also in that headspace."

Ziegler took a break from his secret project to show me around the best loot spots of his Steam library. We talked JRPGs, ARPGs, and the forgotten Bungie game that led him to work on Marathon.

What game are you currently playing?

(Image credit: FromSoftware)I'm playing a couple right now. I'm revisiting Elden Ring Nightreign again. I play it socially with some friends. We're doing a lot of the Deep of Night and purple boss stuff. It's a game that's near and dear to me.

It's funny because my initial reaction to it was like, "What is this game?" But over the course of time, it's combined my love of soulslikes—I really like a lot of soulslikes—with this multiplayer roguelike, where every run you're building a build and trying to conquer the challenge that's in front of you. The level of difficulty keeps it constantly a mastery challenge—which is something that definitely motivates me.

It's a game that's near and dear to me.

Joe Ziegler

A lot of it is playing off of your mastery and understanding of stats that exist in Elden Ring. I played a lot of Elden Ring, so it was easier for me to onboard, and I can imagine for people who have not played a lot of Elden Ring, it's impossible to onboard into. But if you do, you begin theorycrafting a lot of things when you're on your run. You're like, "Oh, should I go for a bleed-based run this time around, am I using the right character with the right arcane stats to do that?" All of your knowledge and all of your capability … come together.

The other game I'm playing is Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Someone called it Race the Spire and I totally agree. It's basically a roguelike racer, and I don't know if it's just the change in pace of playing a racer again, but I think it's been really interesting to see that level of roguelike progression folded into a racer … where all the different components of thinking about your racer become more flexible and interesting from a buildcrafting standpoint.

What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?

(Image credit: Bungie)Oddly enough, I was revisiting Destiny 2. A couple of people I know were getting back into Destiny 2 a little bit, so it was fun to jump in with them and experience going through some stuff.

I have about 730 hours, so I'm not as hardcore as a lot of other people. But D2 is definitely comfort food …. I was originally playing a Warlock. I played a Warlock for quite a few years, and then I just recently went back to playing a Titan, and I was levelling up my Titan again. And I was playing mostly a prismatic spec.

Way back when I was 16, I played a lot of Myth 2 [with] a friend of mine from high school. And oddly enough, it came with a box that had a ticket to go to E3 at the time, which was really crazy. So the first E3 I went to was because Bungie shipped these tickets. I talked to Jason Jones about this, and he was like, "That was all Alex Seropian, and Alex Seropian's marketing mentality was that." So that's how I remember Bungie. Of course I played Halo, just like everybody else who lived in America.

There were a lot of disagreements across the place.

Joe Ziegler

It was the legacy of all those games, Halo to Destiny, that really drove me to work at Bungie … it was actually a couple of friends that I used to work with at Pandemic who were at Bungie who approached me, and one of them was Justin Truman, the former CEO … we started working on something. items.title: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Reviews Make It Sound Like It’s Surprisingly Good
items.author: Ethan Gach
items.summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 isn’t technically out until October 23, but the single-player campaign went live yesterday for anyone who pre-ordered the
items.text:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 isn’t technically out until October 23, but the single-player campaign went live yesterday for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version and a small batch of early reviews have already weighed in on what players can expect. The TL;DR is that it sounds like MW4 gets back to the meat and potatoes of what the franchise’s campaigns do best, even if it might not ultimately rank among the best of them.

There are no scored reviews yet because everyone is waiting for more extensive hands-on time with the multiplayer, including DMZ, before making a final assessment. The in-progress reviews and impressions, however, are much better than the reception last year’s Black Ops 7 got at launch. While that surreal, always-online co-op campaign left many critics genuinely perplexed and disappointed, it sounds like MW4‘s six-hour, 16-mission campaign does exactly what you’d expect from a subseries that now spans seven separate games.

PC Gamer lauded it as a single-player COD experience not to be skipped, and one with some stellar levels that harken back to peak moments from earlier in the series, though it also found the story rushed and unsatisfying, especially the bits that included actor Mads Mikkelsen. “This was billed as the conclusion of the Modern Warfare story that started in 2019, but in practice, it’s more like a sprint to be done with it all,” the site’s Morgan Park wrote.

IGN had similar critiques but was also similarly impressed with the overall package, and pointed to a mission resembling “Korea’s answer to D-Day” as one of the campaign’s large scale highlights. And if you’re “retired” Call of Duty leaker TheGhostOfHope, who correctly predicted Phil Spencer’s eventual departure from Microsoft, well then “This sh*t is f*cking insane man.” Here’s what everyone else is saying so far:

Overall, Modern Warfare 4 wraps up the series with several shocking moments and ends on a high note. The pacing never falters despite the two interwoven storylines and alternating POVs, and the wide variety of missions and locations ensure that the story remains engaging. Modern Warfare 4 is another edge-of-the-seat thrill ride. What distinguishes its campaign from others is a feeling that the devs had more time to think through the experience to create something that can serve as a worthy conclusion for the Modern Warfare series. Because of that, Modern Warfare 4’s campaign ranks as the best we’ve seen since Modern Warfare 2019. – S.E. Doster

Modern Warfare 4 made me feel something for the series again. A consistently strong set of missions manages to juggle a bloated cast successfully, saying goodbye to familiar faces while building impressive bonds with new ones. Its expansive behind-enemy-lines mission that borrows most of its ideas from the DMZ mode is a real highlight, as is whenever its blockbuster ambitions are fulfilled and full-throttle battles break out. It may not have quite enough to be considered amongst the very best Call of Duty campaigns, but if it’s to be the end of this particular saga, then at least Modern Warfare is going out on a high note. – Simon Cardy

This is the most fun I’ve had with a Call of Duty campaign in years, lending mostly to its new, non-elite faces. Over half of the 6-hour campaign revolves around a crew of young South Korean marines (plus a few Americans) running out the clock on their compulsory military service when North Korea suddenly invades. The guys themselves are familiar archetypes—a serious guy, an audience insert who doesn’t talk much, an American who fills every silence with a joke—but they’re basically charming enough that I cared to remember their names. – Morgan Park

When Modern Warfare 4’s missions hit, I’m reminded why the series’ campaigns remain so important in a genre increasingly measured by online success and hours streamed. It might still be junk food – even if this is a higher quality than limp-burger-like Black Ops 7 or Modern Warfare 3’s attempts – but there are glimpses here of how Infinity Ward’s modern approach to a military thriller can still push further. If only they’d let me off the leash a little. – Jake Tucker

There are parts of the story that feel quite emotional and rewarding, while others, such as Mads Mikkelsen’s role in the game, feel a bit undercooked. For what is set to be Infinity Ward closing the door on the Modern Warfare reboot subseries, for now anyway, I believe they have delivered the goods. – Győző “FairyEmpire” Baki

I can say that fans of CoD’s singleplayer components should not be disappointed with what Infinity Ward cooked up here. I think it could go down as one of the better options in the series, and definitely one to remember for righting the ship after years of uncertainty and questionable decision-making. And to top it all off, the game is gorgeous on PC, offering the best visuals in the franchise to date, making it all the more enjoyable throughout. – Scott Duwe

Where Modern Warfare 4 shines most is in its gameplay, which shouldn’t shock anyone. Call of Duty always boasts world-class gunplay, and mechanically it’s still the best at what it does. What might be more impressive to me is the flow of the campaign, however. Most campaigns do the whole “jump between multiple parties shtick”, but MW4 does it with aplomb. The cadence is stellar, with pacing that compliments each chapter. I also love the gameplay variety – rarely did I feel weary of what I was doing. There were slow paced stealth sections, fast moving chase sequences; heck, even a level that had me playing Call of Duty: Frogger Warfare. – David Burdette

While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.
26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.
27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.
28. Zen　(善)
This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.
29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.
30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.
31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.
32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.
Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.
33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.
34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.
35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”
Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.
As a matter of fact, Japanese doesn’t just borrow words from English. To find out more, read our blog: Loan Words in Japanese that Don’t Come from English!

Contact us for more information and make sure to follow our blog for more insight into the Japanese language, culture and society.

Yes, English language borrows a lot of Japanese words. For example, tsunami, tycoon and sudoku came from the Japanese equivalent. English language also retains a lot of original Japanese food-related words, like sushi, katsu and dashi.

items.text:
Welcome to Japan! Along with your first steps in your new life in Tokyo, one of your first priorities is to start learning Japanese. Some of you might already have a certain level of Japanese ability, such as reading and writing hiragana and katakana. But what if you have never learned Japanese before?

When you have completely zero knowledge of Japanese, we recommend you join what is called a Japanese Crash Course, like ones offered at Coto Academy. In 4 weeks, you will learn the fundamentals of Japanese, directly useful for your daily life, including an introduction to hiragana and katakana.

Interested in joining our Japanese Crash Course, or wondering if it’s the right fit for you? We’d love to help! Simply fill out the contact form below, and our English-speaking staff will get back to you shortly.


Get In Touch With Our Team!


What is Japanese Crash Course?

Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course is an intensive, short-term survival program designed specifically for complete beginners and new residents in Japan who need to build functional, everyday Japanese skills as quickly as possible.

AspectDetails

Target LevelZero Beginner (No prior Japanese knowledge required)

Duration1 to 4 weeks (standard core unit runs 4 weeks)

SchedulePart-time intensive (e.g., 4 days/week, 2 hours/day)

LocationsCoto Academy locations (such as Azabu, Iidabashi, Yokohama) & Online

Key Features & Learning Focus


Practical, Conversation-First Curriculum: Focuses on immediate, practical communication rather than heavy grammar theory. Students master key phrases across 9 real-life scenarios, including ordering at restaurants, shopping, asking for directions, self-introductions, and simple daily interactions.

Basic Literacy: Teaches Hiragana and Katakana reading and writing, alongside common Kanji frequently encountered in daily life (such as street signs, menus, and shop notices).

Small Class Sizes: Limited to a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging 3–6), ensuring maximum speaking time and individual feedback from instructors.

Experiential Learning (Tokyo Explorer): Includes interactive outdoor activities where students put their classroom learning to the test in real-world settings like local cafes, supermarkets, and izakayas.


How is Japanese Crash Course Different From Beginner Japanese Lessons?

Japanese Crash Course is a special course designed for individuals who have completely zero knowledge or prior experience in learning Japanese. On the other hand, some beginner Japanese lessons might already expect students to know about basic hiragana and katakana and phrases.

It is important to clarify with your chosen Japanese language school if the beginner lessons they offer are designed for total beginners or not.

Who is This Japanese Crash Course For?

Other than for total beginners, we think Japanese Crash Course is the right fit for you if you:

1. New Arrivals Who Want Practical, Everyday Japanese

If you just arrived in Japan and need to start communicating right away, this course prioritizes real-life interaction over dry theory. Rather than spending weeks on abstract grammar rules, you learn functional phrases you can use immediately for shopping, ordering food, and navigating daily life. The speaking-first approach gets you talking from day one so you feel confident handling everyday tasks.

2. Returning Learners Rebuilding Their Foundation

If you studied Japanese before but took a long break, this course serves as an efficient refresher. It helps you clean up forgotten grammar, review Hiragana and Katakana, and fix gaps in your foundational skills. This reactivates your speaking momentum without forcing you into an overly advanced class.

3. Short-Term Visitors, Tourists & Travelers

If you are visiting Japan for a few weeks or months, you can enjoy a flexible language immersion experience without long-term commitments. Unlike traditional language schools that require 6-month or 1-year visa commitments, you can enroll for short blocks starting from just 1 week. It offers a hands-on way to make your trip richer by learning the language while exploring the country.

What’s The Experiential Learning at Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course?

At Coto Academy, we believe learning a language shouldn’t feel like studying for a history exam. Japanese is a living, breathing tool, and you should get to use it from day one!

That’s where Experiential Learning comes in. Once a week, we take the learning outside! Guided by your teacher, you’ll head out of our campus to complete fun missions like ordering a customized drink, asking a shopkeeper for recommendations, or getting directions to a nearby landmark.

Inside the class, you can expect role-plays like introducing yourself to new friends and handling shopping questions.

Ready to Start Your Japanese Journey?

If you’re excited to learn Japanese by actually living it, our Japanese Crash Course is ready for you! Classes run in small groups to make sure everyone gets plenty of speaking time and personal guidance.

Come join us, meet fellow learners from around the world, and start exploring Japan with confidence!


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


FAQ

Do I need any prior Japanese knowledge to join this course?

No prior experience is necessary! The Japanese Crash Course is specially designed for absolute beginners (Zero Beginner). Whether you haven’t learned a single word yet or only know konnichiwa, our native teachers will walk you through daily essential phrases, as well as hiragana and katakana, step by step.

How long does the course last, and how flexible is the schedule?

We offer high flexibility so you don’t need to make a long-term commitment. While the core unit runs for 4 weeks, you can enroll for anywhere from 1 week to 12 weeks depending on your availability and length of stay in Japan. Classes typically run part-time multiple days a week, making it easy to fit into a busy schedule.

What is the class size like?

To ensure everyone gets personal attention and plenty of speaking time, our classes are kept strictly small, with a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging around 3 to 6 students). You will have continuous opportunities to practice active conversation rather than just passively listening to a lecture.

items.author: Cezary Jan Strusiewicz

items.text:
The new Street Fighter movie (dir. Kitao Sakurai) that opened on October 16 seemingly has one of the easiest jobs in the world. Not only is it based on Capcom’s bestselling fighting game franchise in a time when video game adaptations have proven themselves to be commercially and artistically viable, the bar that the film has to clear is Street Fighter (1994). For years considered one of the worst movies ever made, reactions to it have softened over the years but, at best, they basically boil down to “so bad, it’s kind of good.” And if being better than Steven E. de Souza’s film is a mark of success, then Sakurai’s Street Fighter has already won because it’s not bad. It’s good. Even great at times. But that may not matter, at least for Japan. There are a lot of factors at play here.

VIDEO

For Japan, the Movie to Beat Wasn’t the 1994 Adaptation

Japanese audiences did not love Steven E. de Souza’s Street Fighter, but they also didn’t despise it. There were criticisms at shifting the focus away from Ryu and Ken to the American character Guile (Jean-Claude Van Damme), the B-movie feel of it all and the militaristic guns-blazing vibe to the story. The last one is a common and understandable admonition of the film from a country that still deals with monstrous behavior by some members of the US military. But praise was occasionally given to the scope of the 1994 film as well as some of its sets, effects and performances.

The first Street Fighter adaptation is certified “rotten” on Rotten Tomatoes with a score of 20% from both audiences and critics. But Japanese review sites like KINENOTE or Eiga.com give it a much more lenient 51.5/100 and 2.7/5, respectively. That might be because, before watching Steven E. de Souza’s take on the Capcom property, Japan was treated to what many still consider the best possible adaptation of Street Fighter.

Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie (dir. Gisaburo Sugii) premiered in 1994, a year before the live-action movie was released in Japan. It was a critical and box office success fueled by its faithfulness to the Street Fighter lore and amazing animation. This is the movie that still lives in the pop-culture memory of Japan over 30 years later. This is the movie that Sakurai’s Street Fighter is secretly competing with to attract Japanese fans of the games. And it really did try its hardest.

VIDEO

Street Fighter 2026 Is Uniquely Tailored to Japanese Audiences

Sakurai’s Street Fighter is a live-action movie, but it’s bookended by animated sequences that also pop up throughout the film, courtesy of Titmouse Inc. The scenes are really beautiful, with amazing, fast-paced action. They also technically make a lot of sense since most of the animated parts are flashbacks, which meant that the movie didn’t have to go looking for additional co-stars to play the young Ryu and Ken.

The sequences additionally include a character who might become a big part of the franchise in the future, and introducing him via animation with no lines opens up casting options for a possible sequel. But it still feels like chunks of Street Fighter (2026) are animated to make fans of Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie happy.

On its own, this wouldn’t really be evidence of trying to woo Japanese audiences, but also consider that— slight spoiler alert —the new Guile (Cody Rhodes) is almost comically absent from the movie. The character whose centering was a point of contention for some viewers in Japan actually loses his first tournament fight off-screen. That just smells too much like a deliberate though friendly dig at the 1994 live-action movie. The new film also stars the accomplished Japanese-British actor Andrew Koji as Ryu, casts the popular pro-wrestler Hirooki Goto as E. Honda and even features a prolonged dialogue scene entirely in Japanese. And throughout it all, it doesn’t for one second alienate American viewers.

A Love Letter to the Games

While Koji’s Ryu is one of the central characters of Street Fighter (2026), the movie’s heart is the character’s partner Ken, played by Noah Centineo in a performance of a lifetime. David Dastmalchian as the superpowered dictator M. Bison is also phenomenal, bringing a wonderfully creepy cult leader energy to the big screen, as well as Raúl Juliá’s famous “Tuesday” line from the 1994 film (if you know, you know).

Another thing the film gets right are the fights because it throws realism out the window and fully embraces the wacky atmosphere of the games and the character’s special attacks. But never with a wink or as if it was ashamed that it’s based on a video game. There seems to be genuine love for the Street Fighter games (warts and all) emanating from every scene in Sakurai’s film, which is why it’s such a shame that it might not translate to any kind of success, at least in Japan.

Early Reactions in Japan Are Split

For now, early Japanese reviews of the film are starting to come in, and the verdict so far is divided. Currently, the film’s page on eiga.com, one of Japan’s largest movie sites, is showing a 3.1/5 average. That already beats the 2.7/5 the 1994 film holds on the same site. About half of the scored reviews give 3.5 or 4 stars, one gives a perfect 5, and two give just 1.

The animation, the element the film seems to have built most clearly for Japan, is getting good notices. Four reviewers praise the animated flashbacks, one saying they have more momentum than the live-action scenes, while only one thinks they could have been done in live action. A couple of reviewers say the actors playing Ryu, Ken, Guile and M. Bison are too slim for the game’s muscular fighters. Dastmalchian’s casting as M. Bison is dividing viewers, with some calling the casting genius, while others are saying he lacks menace.

Audiences seem way more responsive to Sakurai’s film in the US where Street Fighter has scored an 84% on Rotten Tomatoes (with the critics giving it just 45%) as of this writing.

As things stand right now, Street Fighter may be heading into the same territory as Mortal Kombat (2021), which was a moderate worldwide success and even got a sequel, but made less than $1 million in Japan and isn’t exactly held up today as the pinnacle of video game adaptations. We’ll have to wait to see what the legacy of the new Street Fighter will ultimately be. In the meantime, catch the film in cinemas to form your own opinion on it.

Related Posts
